content.overview: Section 16 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 bars specific performance in favour of a person who has obtained substituted performance under section 20, who has become incapable of performing or violates an essential term or acts in fraud of the contract or wilfully at variance with it, or who fails to prove performance or continuous readiness and willingness to perform the essential terms. For a money term, the plaintiff must prove that the money was tendered, or that the plaintiff has always been ready and willing to tender it. Terms prevented or waived by the defendant need not be proved as performed. Readiness and willingness is the plaintiff's proof, not a defence the defendant must establish.
content.study: Ask who seeks the decree. A plaintiff who took section 20 relief, broke an essential term, or cannot prove readiness is barred. Averment alone is not the proof the section requires.

learningObjectives: Place the burden of readiness and willingness on the plaintiff.
enhancement.definition: Section 16 identifies the plaintiff who cannot obtain specific performance, including a plaintiff who does not prove readiness and willingness.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Section 10 does not help a plaintiff in section 16. The plaintiff proves the essential terms that were for the plaintiff to perform.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Specific Relief Act, 1963, section 16. Section 20 substituted performance is also a plaintiff bar.
essentialIngredients: No substituted performance obtained by the plaintiff
No violation of an essential term
No fraud on the contract or wilful variance
Proof of performance or continuous readiness and willingness
Money tender, or readiness to tender, if payment is the plaintiff's term
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Clause (a) repeats the section 20 election as a personal bar. Clause (b) covers incapacity, breach of an essential term, fraud on the contract, and wilful acts at variance with or in subversion of the relation the contract intended. Clause (c) is the proof clause. The plaintiff must prove that he has performed, or has always been ready and willing to perform, the essential terms to be performed by him, other than terms the defendant prevented or waived. The explanation says that where a term is payment of money, the plaintiff must prove actual tender or that he has always been ready and willing to tender. It also says the plaintiff need not tender or prove readiness on a term execution of which is a condition precedent to performance by the other, if the plaintiff was ready whenever that condition was fulfilled. The section says prove, so a pleading without proof does not pass clause (c).
examples: The buyer never arranged the price and gives no proof of readiness. Section 16(c) bars the decree.
The seller waived the payment date. The buyer need not prove performance of the waived term.
The buyer has had the property conveyed through a third party under section 20. Section 16(a) bars specific performance.
enhancement.problemApplication: Check substituted performance, essential-term breach, and proof of readiness. Do not shift the readiness burden to the defendant.
distinctions: Section 16 plaintiff bar vs section 14 contract bar
Proof of readiness vs a bare averment
Waived term vs an essential term the plaintiff broke
Money tender vs readiness to tender

keyTakeaways: The plaintiff must prove readiness and willingness.
A money term needs tender or readiness to tender.
A waived or prevented term need not be proved as performed.
Substituted performance is also a plaintiff bar.
Fraud or an essential-term breach bars relief.
